content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors proposed a form of dimensionality reduction algorithm that uses an encoder-decoder structure along with the loss from the Barlow-twin work (Cross-correlation between samples) to learn a lower-dimensional representation of input data where distances are to some degree reflected.
content.main_review:
My review will be short here.

The TLDR is an encoder-decoder structure for dimensionality reduction. The contribution of the authors is to employ the cross-correlation as a loss similar to what devised in the Barlow-twins (as acknowledged by the authors as well). 

I may be very ignorant here but in general I do not think DR in this form is a very interesting problem in the field now.

I also contributions very incremental (although showing that the overall algorithm works is not known to me but on the other hand it was not surprising). 

The way the positive pairs is constructed is the Achilles heel of the algorithm (and similar ones). One can never feed TLDR pure raw data unless Euclidean distances in the input space is meaningful. Authors may argue, it is task-dependent and given another metric, the algorithm may work (which I agree) but as a meta-algorithm, when I think about this construction, I am not 100% satisfied (this is a bit different in self-supervised learning)
content.summary_of_the_review: Again, I do appreciate the efforts put into this work by the authors but unfortunately I do not find the work novel and I also do not think DR in the form considered in this work is a very important task any more.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper97 by Reviewer i8W9

content.title: Authors' Response
content.comment:
We note that the reviewers’ evaluation is mostly based on their assumption that dimensionality reduction is not “a very interesting problem in the field now”. 

We strongly disagree. Dimensionality reduction is still a crucial component in many state-of-the-art pipelines tackling crucial tasks such as image retrieval and text retrieval (as we discuss in the paper), but also in very diverse fields such as biology (drug production, pollution detection, etc.), remote sensing, assisted medical diagnosis, medical imaging analysis, etc. 

> One can never feed TLDR pure raw data unless Euclidean distances in the input space is meaningful

The reviewer is challenging the central assumption behind most of the manifold learning literature, i.e. assuming a locally Euclidean space. We agree that there are cases to which manifold learning cannot be applied, but for all the others, we believe our method is very relevant. 

> showing that the overall algorithm works is not known to me but on the other hand it was not surprising”

We argue that the merits of a detailed experimental analysis should be evaluated according to the amount of insights it provides, not according to how surprising those insights are to the reader.

replying_to: Replying to TLDR: Twin Learning for Dimensionality Reduction
display_title: Official Review of Paper97 by Reviewer X3Uy

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this work, the authors consider the problem of large-scale linear
dimensionality reduction as a replacement for other linear
dimensionality reduction methods such as PCA. To achieve this, the
authors learn an encoder function, via a redundancy reduction loss on
"similar" examples over the training set. The similar examples are
pre-computed offline using simple nearest neighbors on an input
embedding vector from another neural network. Extensive experiments
show that the proposed method is able to outperform PCA and its
variants in two different retrieval tasks.
content.main_review:
In my view the main contribution of this work is to improve upon
previous manifold learning methods, especially Hessel et al., to
achieve dimensionality reduction via a non-contrastive
loss. Specifically, the authors choose the Barlow twins loss (and the
necessary architecture tweaks such as the use of the projector) to
preserve the assumed similarity signal in the input space. The authors
provide enough empirical evidence to show that TLDR is able to do what
is claimed. However, the technical novelty of this work is limited to
just that, offering just a few minor insights on top of prior
work. For instance, the authors point out discussions from prior work
regarding the benefits of non-contrastive learning approaches over
contrastive learning. However, there isn't sufficient
motivation/discussion on the choice of Barlow-Twins loss over other
approaches for this task. The statement "having a highly informative
output space is more important than a highly discriminative one"
provided as a justification has very little basis. Having said that
the experimental results are strong and the authors have conducted
extensive ablation studies to validate the significance of the major
components of their proposed method such as non-contrastive learning,
encoder etc.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The idea of using self-supervised non-contrastive losses for
supervising a dimensionality reduction task is interesting, but the
paper can benefit from a more rigorous analytical treatment. The
experimental results are promising.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper97 by Reviewer X3Uy

content.title: Authors' Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for all their positive comments about our experimental validation, finding our results “strong” and our ablation studies “extensive”.

> There isn’t sufficient motivation/discussion on the choice of Barlow-Twins loss

Thanks for the feedback, we could have discussed this in more depth. For dimensionality reduction, every dimension of the output space counts, and they should be as little correlated as possible. This is exactly what the Barlow-Twins loss implicitly enforces on top of the cross-correlation matrix between the outputs of two identical networks, fed with distorted versions of an image in [Zbontar et. al], and with neighbors in the input space in our work.

display_title: Official Review of Paper97 by Reviewer TKH8

content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript studies the dimensionality reduction problem. The presented method consists two paths to reduce dimentionality by an encoder, then increase the deminsionality by a projector. Finally, correlation is used as a loss to learn the model parameters. Experiments have been done to verify the correctness of the presented method.
content.main_review:
## Strength
1. The experiments have been done in a very comprehensive way, which is good!


## Weakness
1. The idea presented in this manuscript, as illustrated in Figure.1, is very close to the following paper:
[Zbontar et. al, "Barlow Twins: Self-Supervised Learning via Redundancy Reduction", in Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 139:12310-12320, 2021. ](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/zbontar21a.html)
Comparing Figure.1 of this manuscript and Figure.1 of above mentioned paper, we can see that there is almost no difference at all. Considering that the above mentioned paper was just published in a few months ago, the contribution of this manuscript is rather limited.

2. Even though there was not the above mentioned paper published in ICML 2021, the idea of this paper is rather simple: (1) an encoder to (nonlinearly) reduce dimentionality, followed by a projector to raise the dimensionality again, (2) CCA, as show in Eq.(1), is used to utilize data correlations. So the novelty of this manuscript, as well as the ICML paper mentioned above, indeed is questionable in terms of methodology. The only possible contribution of this manuscript, as well as the ICML paper mentioned above, may be its simplicity, which may lead to better computational efficiency for dealing with big data. Yet, when encoder is used, it is hard to see it is possible to have a fast solution, compared to traditional PCA (or kernel PCA), ICA, CCA, in terms of computational speed. Most importantly, it seems computational speed is not verified in experiments.

3. Although the experiments have been done pretty comprehensive (which is a plus), some important aspects are not evaluated.
    1. Considering an encoder can learn nonlinear dimenionality reduction, it is important to compare the presented method against kernel PCA.
    2. It may be good to compare encoder-decoder as well.
content.summary_of_the_review: This manuscript studies the dimensionality reduction problem by presenting a two-path strategy to use CCA loss, in which each path consists of an encoder to reduce dimentionality and a projector to increase the deminsionality. A similar idea has been published in ICML 2021 and some important aspects are not evaluated in experiments.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper97 by Reviewer TKH8

content.title: Authors' Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their positive comments on our experimental evaluation.

> The idea presented in this manuscript, as illustrated in Figure.1, is very close to Zbontar et al [...] Comparing Figure.1 of this manuscript and Figure.1 of the above-mentioned paper, we can see that there is almost no difference at all.

As mentioned in the joint answer above, and at many places in the paper, we indeed build on top of [Zbontar et al], citing it every time it is necessary, including in our teaser figure. We made the latter on purpose similar to the one in [Zbontar et al], in order to ease the understanding of our paper for readers already familiar with this prior work, and highlight the small but important differences that enable this architecture and loss to be used to a different task, and to very different domains, such as natural language processing.

> “the novelty of this manuscript, as well as the ICML paper mentioned above [Zbontar et al] is questionable in terms of methodology”, “only contribution of this manuscript and the ICML paper may be its simplicity

We refer the reader to [Zbontar et al] for the contributions of the Barlow Twins (BT) visual representation learning method, discussing those is out of scope. Our technical contributions on top of that paper are: a different input space, a different strategy to define positive pairs, a new encoder architecture. Those seemingly simple changes enable us to entirely revisit a visual representation learning method, and tailor it for dimensionality reduction that is independent of the nature/modality of the input data.

> when encoder is used, it is hard to see if it is possible to have a fast solution, compared to traditional PCA (or kernel PCA), ICA, CCA

We’ll discuss the encoding/test time complexity, which is the most crucial aspect for the large-scale applications TLDR is suitable for. With a linear or factorized linear encoder, TLDR requires as much computation as PCA/ICA/CCA; it is a linear operation. Our paper focuses on linear dimensionality reduction, and reports only very few results for the non-linear one, only for the sake of the discussion, which is why we didn’t report any results with Kernel PCA. We will consider this comparison in the future, but expect the conclusions to be similar to those of our comparisons with UMAP kernel, LTSA, and LLA (Figure 5a).

display_title: Very few actionable or rebuttable points - withdrawing our submission

content.title: Very few actionable or rebuttable points - withdrawing our submission
content.comment:
We want to thank all reviewers for taking the time to review our work. Given that we overall got low scores with high confidence and there are very few actionable or rebuttable points that could change the reviewers’ mind, we choose to withdraw our submission. 

We have taken note that all reviewers found the work to lack technical novelty. We agree with them that our work is strongly based on Zbontar et. al, "Barlow Twins: Self-Supervised Learning via Redundancy Reduction", a connection which we openly and precisely discuss in the paper. Still, we tackle a different task, dimensionality reduction, and we believe that this paper proposes an unconventional yet successful method to attack this fundamental task, which is still at the core of many state-of-the-art pipelines. Although seemingly small, the architectural differences between TLDR and the Barlow Twins method enable us to use this highly scalable self-supervised optimization framework proposed for visual representation learning for dimensionality reduction and on a much wider set of domains, such as natural language processing. 

We believe that the TLDR method proposed in this work is a very useful tool applicable to a wide range of domains, and of practical applications.

We respond to some of the reviewers’ comments below.
